title: CNAS Insights | Sovereign AI's Second Wave Is Coming Into View
gist: CNAS's Sovereign AI Index shows government-backed sovereign AI projects have surged from 1 in January 2023 to 184 across 67 countries by mid-2026, with growth increasingly driven by infrastructure buildouts in lower-income countries and a small but growing foothold for Chinese open-weight base models like Alibaba's Qwen.

themes.theme: Scale and Pace of the Sovereign AI Wave

insights.claim: CNAS's Sovereign AI Index, which tracks every government-backed sovereign AI project since 2023, has grown from a single project in January 2023 to 184 projects across 67 countries by mid-2026.
insights.speaker: CNAS
insights.so_what: Establishes sovereign AI as a structural, accelerating global trend rather than a niche policy fad, relevant to national AI-infrastructure and localization-driven capex forecasts.
insights.locator: In January 2023, the index highlighted just a single project

insights.claim: The index tracked 41 new sovereign AI projects in the first half of 2026 alone, more than were launched in all of 2024, and second only to the 51 projects added in the second half of 2025.
insights.speaker: CNAS
insights.so_what: Momentum is still accelerating rather than plateauing, implying continued near-term demand for localized AI compute and data infrastructure.
insights.locator: The index tracked 41 new projects in the first half of 2026

insights.claim: Despite broad global adoption, diffusion remains shallow: 40 percent of all countries tracked in the index back just a single sovereign AI project.
insights.speaker: CNAS
insights.so_what: Most national sovereign AI efforts are token, single-project commitments rather than deep programs, useful for separating genuine strategic bets from symbolic ones.
insights.locator: the diffusion of sovereign AI remains broad but shallow

insights.claim: Sovereign AI is no longer concentrated among wealthy nations: from 16 governments (mostly in Europe, East Asia and the Gulf) in 2023, the roster expanded to 67 countries plus the EU by mid-2026, including 10 first-time entrants from lower- and middle-income economies (Cambodia, the Dominican Republic, Egypt, Ghana, Nepal, Pakistan, Papua New Guinea, Paraguay, the Philippines, and Uruguay).
insights.speaker: CNAS
insights.so_what: Signals a new addressable market of developing-economy government buyers for AI infrastructure and compute vendors, beyond the traditional wealthy-country customer base.
insights.locator: Sovereign AI is no longer the preserve of mostly wealthy countries

insights.claim: At the halfway point of 2026, one in three countries worldwide was pursuing sovereign AI in some form, representing 90 percent of global GDP outside the United States and China.
insights.speaker: CNAS
insights.so_what: Frames sovereign AI as a near-universal policy priority across the rest-of-world economy, a durable secular theme rather than a fringe trend.
insights.locator: representing 90 percent of global GDP outside the United States and China

insights.claim: Papua New Guinea launched the first sovereign AI project tracked in the Pacific, and the Dominican Republic launched the first tracked in the Caribbean, marking new regional frontiers for the trend.
insights.speaker: CNAS
insights.so_what: Early-mover data points for regions previously absent from AI infrastructure investment maps.
insights.locator: New regions are also putting down first markers

insights.claim: Existing sovereign AI leaders are deepening commitments rather than just spreading wider: roughly 70 percent of new first-half-2026 projects came from countries already in the index, and just 10 countries account for nearly 40 percent of all tracked projects.
insights.speaker: CNAS
insights.so_what: Investment and demand are concentrating among a core group of repeat sovereign-AI spenders, useful for prioritizing coverage of government AI-procurement pipelines.
insights.locator: Sovereign AI leaders are doubling down

insights.claim: The Asia-Pacific region added more sovereign AI projects than Europe for the first time in the first half of 2026 (16 versus 13), with India alone hosting 11 projects, more than any other country, propelled by the February 2026 AI Impact Summit in Delhi.
insights.speaker: CNAS
insights.so_what: India is emerging as the single largest national sovereign-AI buyer and builder, a market to watch for compute vendors and model licensors.
insights.locator: The Asia-Pacific is an emerging hub for sovereign AI

insights.claim: India added four infrastructure programs in the first half of 2026 alone, including one of the country's largest AI compute clusters, while the Delhi summit showcased homegrown models Sarvam and Param2 that the index has tracked since 2025.
insights.speaker: CNAS
insights.so_what: Concrete named Indian model and infrastructure programs worth tracking as proxies for India's AI self-sufficiency trajectory.
insights.locator: India added four infrastructure programs, including one of the country's largest

insights.claim: Infrastructure projects (AI data centers, compute-access programs) rose to 80 percent of all new sovereign AI projects in the first half of 2026, up from 62 percent in the prior six months, with Ghana and South Africa launching Sub-Saharan Africa's first compute-focused projects tracked by the index.
insights.speaker: CNAS
insights.so_what: The overwhelming majority of sovereign AI capital is flowing into physical compute and data-center buildout rather than models or data, directly investable in power, land and hardware supply chains, including new African markets.
insights.locator: Infrastructure projects still account for the largest share

insights.claim: Data projects (national training datasets, data-sharing platforms) remain the smallest category, just 5 percent of new first-half-2026 projects, with only one in five tracked governments backing any project with an explicit data component.
insights.speaker: CNAS
insights.so_what: Identifies a persistently underinvested layer of the sovereign AI stack, a potential future growth segment as infrastructure buildouts mature.
insights.locator: Data projects, which build national datasets for model training

themes.theme: Model Layer: US Dominance, Rising Chinese Foothold, and the Capability Tradeoff

insights.claim: Most sovereign AI model projects with disclosed bases are fine-tuned versions of foreign open-weight models rather than built from scratch, and three-fifths of these foreign bases are American, with Meta's Llama the most-used base model and France's Mistral and Google's Gemma tied for second.
insights.speaker: CNAS
insights.so_what: US open-weight models, especially Llama, remain the default substrate for global sovereign AI, a soft-power and ecosystem lock-in for US AI labs even amid sovereignty rhetoric.
insights.locator: Sovereign AI model projects still rely largely on American foundations

insights.claim: Chinese base models were largely absent before 2025 but now appear in six countries via two labs: Alibaba's Qwen is used in Egypt, Singapore, Thailand, Uganda and the UAE, while Kazakhstan's national model AlemLLM was built with direct technical support from China's 01.AI on a proprietary Chinese base.
insights.speaker: CNAS
insights.so_what: Early but concrete evidence of Chinese open-weight models gaining share in the sovereign AI base-model market, a competitive threat to Meta, Google and Mistral's current dominance worth monitoring for share shifts.
insights.locator: Chinese models were largely absent before 2025 but now appear

insights.claim: The number of sovereign AI models built entirely from scratch (not fine-tuned on a foreign base) has roughly doubled every year and now represents about 40 percent of all model projects, a new high, as countries worry about being cut off from foreign providers.
insights.speaker: CNAS
insights.so_what: Rising 'from scratch' share signals growing distrust of dependency on foreign AI providers, a secular tailwind for domestic AI chip and compute demand even at the cost of capability.
insights.locator: The total number of 'from scratch' sovereign AI models tracked

insights.claim: About two-thirds of 'from scratch' sovereign models have fewer than 70 billion parameters, versus the 2.8 trillion-parameter Kimi K3 from China's Moonshot AI, showing these models lag far behind the frontier despite the effort invested.
insights.speaker: CNAS
insights.so_what: Sets a scale benchmark showing most sovereign models are non-frontier, implying limited near-term competitive threat to frontier labs but a large addressable market for smaller-scale AI infrastructure and tooling providers.
insights.locator: About two-thirds have fewer than 70 billion parameters

insights.claim: Switzerland's from-scratch Apertus model underperforms the frontier overall, but the Canton of Ticino fine-tuned it into a confidential-document translator that outperforms Meta's Llama Scout for that specific task, illustrating the tradeoff of accepting diminished general capability for domestic control.
insights.speaker: CNAS
insights.so_what: A concrete case showing sub-frontier sovereign models can still win narrow, high-value government use cases against larger foreign models, a template other governments may replicate.
insights.locator: Take Switzerland's Apertus model, which it trained from scratch

insights.claim: Only a handful of jurisdictions, India, South Korea, the United Kingdom, and Taiwan, have operational sovereign AI programs across all three stack layers (compute, models, and data), suggesting a growing divergence between full-stack leaders and a much larger cohort of one-off, single-layer projects.
insights.speaker: CNAS
insights.so_what: Identifies the small set of countries pursuing comprehensive AI self-sufficiency, the most credible long-term competitors and customers for full-stack AI ecosystems.
insights.locator: Few countries have sovereign AI projects across the stack

insights.claim: Sub-national sovereign AI activity is accelerating sharply: five regions (Bavaria in Germany, Tamil Nadu and Odisha in India, Sarawak in Malaysia, and Ulsan in South Korea) launched six new sub-national projects in the first half of 2026 alone, as many as were added in the previous three years combined.
insights.speaker: CNAS
insights.so_what: Sovereign AI investment decision-making is fragmenting below the national level, creating a new tier of sub-national government buyers and regulators to track.
insights.locator: The first half of 2026 saw six new sub-national projects

insights.claim: Industry-specific sovereign AI projects, which began appearing in 2025 (e.g., a Turkish program funding health and finance models, a French defense AI program), became more common in 2026, with new examples including a shipbuilding foundation model in South Korea, a financial-sector model in Taiwan, and a defense data platform in Ukraine.
insights.speaker: CNAS
insights.so_what: Sector-specific sovereign AI (defense, finance, shipbuilding) is an emerging vertical for specialized AI vendors targeting regulated, high-value industries with strong incentives to control proprietary data.
insights.locator: Critical industries are embracing sovereign AI

insights.claim: The report's authors argue Washington should abandon the goal of full global adoption of the American AI stack, since 'no country — not even America's closest allies — will accept that level of dependence,' and instead should aim to become the world's sovereign partner of choice by helping shape partner AI strategies and making US AI-stack access more predictable and reliable.
insights.speaker: Pablo Chavez, Vivek Chilukuri & Ruby Scanlon (CNAS)
insights.so_what: A direct policy prescription with commercial implications: US AI vendors offering sovereignty-friendly partnership terms, rather than pushing full-stack dependency, may better capture this large addressable global market.
insights.quote: No country–not even America's closest allies–will accept that level of dependence.
insights.locator: Washington should recognize that full adoption of the American AI stack
